# 5.2 - Sampling Methods {.unnumbered}

A school has 1,200 students. The principal wants to ask 60 of them about the new schedule.

If she asks the first 60 students who walk in the door, she gets only the students who come early. They may not be like everyone else. The best ways to choose use **chance**, so no group is favored.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I name and describe simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic, and convenience samples.
- [ ] I tell stratified and cluster samples apart.
- [ ] I use a random digit table to choose a sample.
- [ ] I choose a good sampling method for a situation.
:::

### 5.2.1 - Five Ways to Choose a Sample

| Method | How it works | Example (60 of 1,200) |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple random sample (SRS)** | Every group of the same size has the same chance of being chosen. Like drawing names from a hat. | Number the students 1 to 1,200. A random number generator picks 60 numbers. |
| **Stratified** | Split the population into groups (**strata**). People in the same group are alike in some way. Take a random sample from **each** group. | Randomly pick 15 students from each grade: 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th. |
| **Cluster** | Split the population into groups (**clusters**). Randomly pick some **whole** groups. | Randomly pick 3 homerooms. Ask everyone in them. |
| **Systematic** | Pick a random start. Then take every $k$th person. $k$ is the population size divided by the sample size. | Start at a random student from 1 to 20. Then take every 20th student on the list. |
| **Convenience** (bad) | Take whoever is easy to reach. | Ask the first 60 students who walk in the door. |

:::{.gotcha title="Stratified or cluster?"}
- **Stratified:** a **few** from **every** group.
- **Cluster:** **everyone** from a **few** groups.
:::

:::{.you-try title="A school has a list of its 1,200 students. Describe a systematic sample of 80 students."}
$k = 1{,}200 \div 80 = 15$.

Pick a random start from 1 to 15. Then take every 15th student on the list.
:::

***

### 5.2.2 - Using a Random Digit Table

Each digit in the table is random. For 2-digit numbers, read the digits in pairs.

| | |
|---|---|
| Row 1 | `52601 81590 83016 61318 60913 90996 03082 46281` |
| Row 2 | `94821 99351 81909 37865 79754 32319 48757 49118` |
| Row 3 | `62527 60189 55597 97114 71049 74650 75291 70342` |

**Example:** Choose 3 of 25 students, numbered 01 to 25. Use row 1.

Pairs: 52, 60, **18**, **15**, 90, 83, **01**, ...

Skip numbers over 25. Skip repeats. The sample is students **18, 15, and 01**.

:::{.think title="Why use chance at all?"}
People who choose a sample by hand often choose people who are easy to reach. They may choose people like themselves. They do not mean to do it. Chance does not pick favorites, so a random sample is not biased toward any group.
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Naming Methods**

1. Name the sampling method.

   a. A store gives a survey to every 10th customer, starting with a randomly chosen customer from the first 10.

   b. A city randomly picks 5 of its 40 neighborhoods and surveys every home in those 5.

   c. A teacher puts all 28 names in a hat and draws 6.

   d. A college randomly picks 50 first-year, 50 second-year, 50 third-year, and 50 fourth-year students.

   e. A reporter asks people walking past a coffee shop.

2. A class has 30 students, numbered 01 to 30. Use **row 3** of the random digit table to choose 4 students.

***

**Choosing a Method**

3. A school wants to survey 100 of its 1,000 students about sports. About half of the students play a sport.

   a. Describe how to take a stratified sample.

   b. Why might a stratified sample be better than an SRS here?

4. A farmer has 50 rows of corn. She wants to check 500 plants for insects. She randomly picks 5 rows and checks every plant in them.

   a. What method is this?

   b. Why would a farmer choose this method?

5. Maya wants to know how students feel about school lunch. She surveys the first 40 students in the lunch line.

   a. What method is this? What is the problem?

   b. Describe a better way for Maya to choose 40 students.
